steps.title: Choosing map or filter for iterable transformations

blocks.text: `map(function, iterable)` lazily applies a callable to successive items, yielding results.
`filter(predicate, iterable)` lazily keeps items whose predicate is true; `filter(None, iterable)` keeps truthy items.
`filter(predicate, iterable)` corresponds to `(item for item in iterable if predicate(item))`.
`[function(item) for item in iterable if predicate(item)]` materializes a transform-and-filter list; it can replace a map/filter composition when clearer.
To preserve lazy traversal, use a parenthesized generator expression rather than a list comprehension.

left.code:
def positive(value):
    return value > 0

def double(value):
    return value * 2

values = [3, -1, 2]
lazy = map(double, filter(positive, values))
print(list(lazy))

right.code:
def positive(value):
    return value > 0

def double(value):
    return value * 2

values = [3, -1, 2]
stored = [double(value) for value in values if positive(value)]
lazy = (double(value) for value in values if positive(value))

blocks.takeaway: List materializes; the parenthesized form stays lazy.
